lines.text: Three ionised layers over one transmitter. The heights are to scale with each other.
A little power crawls along the ground and is gone within a couple of hundred miles.
The rest goes up, is bent back by the F2 layer, and lands a long way off. One hop.
Between the two there is nothing at all.
The station five hundred miles away can be unreachable; the one two thousand miles away is loud.
Raise the frequency and the ray goes deeper before it turns, and lands further away.
Push it too far and the layer cannot turn it back at all. The signal leaves.
Now a flare goes off on the Sun.
Its X-rays cross in eight minutes and stop in the D region — the lowest layer.
D stops being a mirror and starts being a sponge.
Absorption goes as one over frequency squared. Four megahertz never gets out of the D region.
Seven is badly weakened. Fourteen is still working.
Every HF path has a ceiling and a floor. You work between them.
The flare barely moves the ceiling. It lifts the floor.
The low end goes first, then the middle.
When the floor reaches the ceiling there is no usable frequency left.
